title: An adaptive fractional state links circuit mechanisms to cortical dynamics across the visual hierarchy
abstract: Cortical circuits must respond flexibly to new inputs while integrating information about the past, yet the way in which neural activity reconciles these competing demands remains unclear. Combining Neuropixels recordings from six mouse visual areas with mechanistic circuit modeling, we identify a dynamical regime in which heavy-tailed superdiffusive fluctuations coexist with long-range temporal dependence and oscillations. We formalize this regime as the adaptive fractional (AF) state, using an effective mean-field theory in which spatial and temporal fractional derivatives capture heavy-tailed excursions and long-range memory, respectively. We find that dynamical exponents characterizing the AF state vary systematically across the visual hierarchy: higher visual areas exhibit weaker superdiffusion and stronger temporal memory. In the circuit model, this hierarchical shift emerges from a progressive weakening of effective inhibition. These findings extend the classical hierarchy of timescales to a hierarchy of dynamical regimes and suggest that the AF state allows cortical areas to jointly express rapid responses and long-term temporal integration.
summary: This work characterizes the 'adaptive fractional (AF) state' in the visual cortex, a dynamical regime defined by the simultaneous presence of superdiffusion, long-range memory, and oscillations. By applying a bi-fractional mean-field theory, the authors show that the quantitative signatures of this state vary systematically across the visual hierarchy, suggesting that circuit maturation involves tuning these fractional dynamical parameters.
main_problem: The paper investigates how cortical circuits reconcile the competing demands of responding flexibly to new inputs while integrating information about the past (long-term temporal integration).
main_result: Cortical activity exhibits an 'adaptive fractional (AF) state,' characterized by the coexistence of heavy-tailed superdiffusive excursions, long-range temporal memory, and oscillations. This state varies systematically across the visual hierarchy, correlating with changes in effective inhibition.
method: The authors combine analysis of Neuropixels recordings (LFP/spiking activity) with the development and application of a bi-fractional neural sampling (bFNS) effective mean-field theory.
model_or_system: The system is the mouse visual cortex, analyzed using data from six visual areas. The theoretical framework is the bi-fractional model, which uses spatial and temporal fractional derivatives to capture non-Gaussian excursions and long-range memory.
key_observables: Superdiffusion exponent ($a$), temporal fractional order (long-range memory), oscillation frequencies ($	heta, \gamma$), excess kurtosis ($\kappa$), and the Fano factor ($F(	au)$).
important_parameters: The dynamical exponents ($a, b, c$) are key, showing a systematic shift across the visual hierarchy, linked to progressive weakening of effective inhibition.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed dynamics can be effectively described by a bi-fractional process, and the interpretation of exponents relies on fitting these fractional models to empirical data.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate LFP step-size distributions showing heavy tails, Power Spectral Density decomposition into oscillatory and aperiodic parts, and plots showing the systematic variation of dynamical exponents across different visual areas and cortical layers.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem (reconciling flexibility and memory), introduces the AF state concept, details the bi-fractional model formulation, presents experimental evidence from LFP/spiking data showing the coexisting signatures, and finally maps the systematic variation of these signatures across the visual hierarchy.
why_interesting: The use of fractional calculus to model complex, non-Markovian dynamics in biological systems provides a powerful mathematical tool for understanding emergent collective behavior, which has parallels in modeling complex quantum many-body dynamics or open quantum systems.
